The Cape sugarbird Promerops cafer exhibits a set of well-documented life-history traits that reflect its specialization on nectarivory within the fynbos biome. In a study of a coastal population, researchers recorded the fledging milestone, which occurs approximately 20 days after hatching [tx = approximately 20 days after hatching] under the warm thermal conditions typical of active-season metabolism, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The first successful breeding attempt by these birds generally takes place about 365 days after hatching [tR = about 365 days after hatching], suggesting that while they are capable of breeding in their first year, most individuals do not initiate reproduction until their second austral at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]spring. This relatively early age at first reproduction is consistent with that of other small-bodied passerines inhabiting seasonal environments, where annual fluctuations in flower abundance are a key driver of reproductive timing.

Sexual maturity is attained quite early in this species, with puberty estimated at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth] based on observations of gonadal development in captive individuals at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid physiological maturation is unusual among nectarivores of similar mass and may be an adaptation to the unpredictable timing of nectar pulses. Body mass at the onset of independence is modest, as newly hatched nestlings weigh approximately 3.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.6 grams], a value that is typical for altricial passerines of this lineage. The initial weight of a freshly laid egg, representing the earliest measurable stage, averages 3.81 grams [Ww0 = 3.81 grams], reflecting the considerable maternal investment in yolk and albumen for a bird whose adult size remains relatively small. Nestlings grow rapidly on a diet of insects and nectar.

Adult body size exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, which is common among members of the Promeropidae. The wet weight attained by adult females, representing their asymptotic body mass, is approximately 32.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 32.2 grams], while males are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 37.5 grams [Wwi = 37.5 grams]. This 16% difference in mass likely relates to the role of male territorial defense in the lek-like mating system of this species, where larger males outcompete smaller rivals for access to prime nectar-rich territories that attract females. In comparison, the closely related malachite sunbird Nectarinia famosa shows a smaller degree of sexual size dimorphism, suggesting that the selective pressures on body size in the sugarbird may be more closely tied to competition for access to prime feeding territories rather than to aerial displays alone. The energetic demands of sustaining such a body size require high daily nectar intake.

Under the stable thermal conditions of a controlled environment set to 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which simulates the elevated body temperature typical of active foraging periods, the maximum reproductive rate of this species can be expressed in terms of its two components: females typically lay a clutch of 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and they may produce up to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 2 clutches per year] when nectar resources are abundant and predation pressure is low. This rate of two broods annually is notable for a passerine of this size, as many temperate-zone insectivores only manage a single brood. However, field observations suggest that a second clutch is not always attempted, especially in drier years. The incubation of eggs lasts approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that is consistent with other small passerines of the region and supports successful embryonic development.

Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated based on banding records of the closely related violet-capped woodhoopoe Anthobaphes violacea, which suggest an extrapolated lifespan for the Cape sugarbird of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under natural conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small passerines that face high predation risks from raptors and snakes.
